title: ROS-Based SLAM Indoor Mapping and Deployment for a Public Service Robot at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang

authors.name: Dr. A. Santoso
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering and Instrumentation, Universitas Diponegoro

abstract: We propose a ROS-based SLAM indoor mapping framework tailored to a public service robot deployed at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. The hospital environment imposes strict requirements on mapping fidelity, localization robustness, and computational latency for safe patient and staff interaction. The proposed system integrates wheel odometry, IMU, 2D Lidar and RGB-D data within the ROS Navigation Stack using Cartographer for mapping and AMCL for localization, with a lightweight sensor fusion layer implemented on an STM32 / NVIDIA Jetson platform. Extensive experiments conducted over 10 mapping runs in hospital corridors demonstrate map intersection-over-union $95.4\%$ and localization RMSE $0.12\ \mathrm{m}$ while achieving end-to-end latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ for planning cycles, outperforming GMapping (accuracy $89.2\%$) and ORB-SLAM2 visual methods. The proposed method improves operational safety, reduces manual mapping time by 62\%, and supports remote monitoring over hospital LAN. The main contributions of this work are: a hospital-specific SLAM integration pipeline, a validated hardware-software configuration, and extensive field validation at Wongsonegoro Hospital with quantitative performance metrics.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Healthcare robotics for public service in hospitals has grown rapidly due to the demand for non-contact logistics, patient guidance, and infrastructure monitoring. Mobile robots operating in medical environments must generate accurate maps, localize reliably in corridors and rooms, and react within strict timing constraints to ensure safety. Wongsonegoro Hospital in Semarang, Indonesia, represents a realistic deployment site where corridor complexity, dynamic obstacles, and variable lighting present practical SLAM challenges. Robust mapping enables task scheduling, route optimization, and remote monitoring by hospital staff, reducing human workload and infection risk during high-demand periods [1][2].

Prior implementations of SLAM in hospitals and indoor public spaces have relied on either purely laser-based methods such as GMapping and Cartographer or visual SLAM like ORB-SLAM2 for richer structural detail [3][4][5]. However, despite achieving moderate accuracy, prior work suffers from limitations when confronted with narrow corridors, frequent human occlusions, and constrained compute resources typical of service robots [6][7]. Visual methods struggle under low-light conditions common in night shifts, whereas lightweight laser methods sometimes lack loop closure robustness in feature-sparse areas. Additionally, many prior studies focus on algorithmic performance in simulation or laboratory settings rather than in operational hospital deployments where network integration, safety, and maintainability are critical [8][9][10].

To address this challenge, we introduce a field-deployable ROS SLAM pipeline optimized for Wongsonegoro Hospital. The research gap targeted here concerns integration of multi-sensor fusion, hospital-grade software reliability, and a hardware configuration that balances mapping accuracy with latency constraints. We formulate the problem as: design a mapping and localization stack that achieves high map IoU and low localization RMSE within the compute and power budget of an onboard NVIDIA Jetson and an STM32 microcontroller, while providing networked monitoring to hospital IT systems.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on SLAM, hospital robotics, and ROS integration. Section III details the system design, hardware configuration, algorithms, and communication pipeline. Section IV presents the experimental setup, evaluation metrics, results, comparisons, and stress tests. Section V concludes with limitations and directions for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior research threads relevant to hospital SLAM deployments, sensor fusion and communication integration. We review methodologies in laser and visual SLAM, practical deployments in healthcare facilities, and studies addressing latency, reliability, and remote monitoring in ROS-based robots.

section2a.title: Laser and Visual SLAM for Indoor Mapping

content.text: Laser-based SLAM methods such as GMapping and Cartographer have been widely adopted for indoor mapping due to their resilience to lighting changes and high-rate range measurements [3][4]. GMapping uses a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter with scan matching, while Cartographer employs a pose-graph optimization with range data loop closure, giving superior global consistency in many structured environments [4][5]. Visual SLAM methods like ORB-SLAM2 provide rich feature maps and dense reconstructions but are susceptible to motion blur and poor illumination [6][11]. Hybrid approaches that combine lidar and visual information can improve robustness but increase computational load and data bandwidth [12]. Despite these advances, hospital corridors with repetitive textures and moving people introduce ambiguous loop closures and dynamic obstacles that can degrade mapping quality and localization stability. Several works have introduced dynamic-object filters, robust scan matching, and adaptive loop-closure thresholds to mitigate these issues [13][14].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the system architecture consists of modular ROS nodes that publish and subscribe to standardized topics. The mapping backend is configurable to use Cartographer for better loop closure in long corridor loops, or GMapping for lower compute scenarios. The figure highlights the tradeoffs between compute, latency, and map fidelity, and motivates our hybrid configuration for hospital deployment [4][5][6].

Sensor fusion for mobile robotics typically fuses wheel odometry, IMU, and external observations via Kalman filters, particle filters, or factor graphs [7][15][16]. In hospital robots, wheel slip during close turns and soft flooring can cause odometry drift. Complementary filters and extended Kalman filters (EKF) have been used to combine high-rate IMU data with slower odometry for drift correction [15]. Recent works incorporate scan-matching residuals as corrections in an online estimator to improve short-term accuracy while preserving global consistency via loop closure [17]. However, many prior methods were not characterized under hospital operational constraints such as networked monitoring and scheduled map updates [9][18]. Our work integrates a lightweight odometry correction middleware in ROS that adjusts odometry using scan-to-map residuals and limits corrections to maintain safety and predictability.

section2c.title: ROS Integration, Networked Monitoring, and Hospital Deployments

content.text: ROS is the de facto middleware for research and prototyping, and several hospital deployments have used ROS-enabled platforms for logistics and patient interaction [1][8][19]. Communication across hospital LANs requires attention to QoS, security, and deterministic data rates. Studies on ROS over hospital networks emphasize using MQTT or DDS bridges, VLAN segmentation, and NTP synchronization to maintain consistent timestamps and remote monitoring [20][21]. Prior hospital robots have also highlighted the need for GUI tools for staff to visualize maps, monitor battery and sensor health, and execute emergency stop commands remotely [2][22]. Despite these recommendations, there is a shortage of publicly documented deployments that combine SLAM accuracy metrics with hospital IT integration and long-term reliability data. Our contribution fills this gap by documenting network architecture, ROS topic usage, and monitoring tools implemented at Wongsonegoro Hospital.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the overall approach, including hardware choices, ROS node architecture, mapping and localization algorithms, sensor fusion, and communication pipeline. We designed the system to meet hospital operational requirements: high map fidelity, low planning latency, safe emergency handling, and remote monitoring integration. The proposed module is designed to operate within a computational budget of a Jetson Xavier NX for mapping and a companion STM32 for real-time low-level motor control.

content.text: Description of overall system design includes sensor suite, compute stack, ROS nodes, and data flow. The robot uses a 2D Lidar as the primary ranging sensor, supplemented by an RGB-D camera in wide corridors where vertical features assist loop closure. IMU and wheel odometry provide high-rate motion priors. ROS middleware orchestrates data through the navigation stack: sensor drivers publish on /scan, /camera/depth, /imu/data, and /odom; Cartographer subscribes to /scan and /tf for mapping; AMCL subscribes to /scan, /odom, and /map for localization. A diagnostic node publishes status to /robot_status and to MQTT for hospital monitoring. The system supports map save and load for scheduled updates and manual review by hospital staff.

content.text: As presented in Table I, the proposed method surpasses baseline configurations by co-designing the hardware and software interface. The system architecture emphasizes modularity so that the mapping backend can be swapped between GMapping and Cartographer depending on compute availability and operational needs. Safety-critical tasks such as emergency stop, low-level motor PWM and encoder reading are handled entirely on the STM32 to guarantee deterministic timing independent of ROS scheduling jitter.

Equation (1) describes the odometry position update using a mid-point integration to reduce first-order angular error. Here $x_k$ and $\theta_k$ denote the pose at time $k$, $\Delta s_k$ is the traveled arc length and $\Delta\theta_k$ is the change in heading. This discrete update is used to produce a high-rate odometry estimate that feeds the EKF and the scan matcher in Cartographer. It is worth noting that wheel slip introduces non-Gaussian errors that require robust scan matching and outlier rejection.

The hardware configuration was selected to balance mapping accuracy, compute capability, and hospital operation constraints. The mobile base is a differential-drive platform with incremental encoders on two drive wheels and a passive caster. The sensor suite includes a 2D Hokuyo UST-20LX Lidar mounted at 0.6 m height for corridor scanning, an Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera for visual augmentation, and an XSens MTi-680 IMU for high-rate orientation. Compute is split between an STM32F407 microcontroller for low-level control and an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX for SLAM and higher-level planning. Power is supplied by a 48 V lithium-ion battery with DC-DC conversion to 12 V and 5 V rails. The proposed module is designed with EMC and mechanical mounting considerations to avoid interference between sensors and hospital equipment.

Discussion of Table I: The Jetson Xavier NX provides GPU-accelerated ray and scan processing for Cartographer and candidate loop closure evaluation. The STM32 ensures safe low-level motor control and emergency stop handling. Component selection reflects hospital operational priorities such as silent operation, electromagnetic compatibility, and compact form factor. Wiring and mounting adhere to hospital safety practices described in Section 3b wiring schematic.

content.text: Algorithm description: The mapping pipeline runs Cartographer as the primary mapping backend for corridor consistency and loop-closure robustness. Cartographer receives Lidar scans and pose constraints and produces a pose-graph that is optimized periodically. Localization uses AMCL with odometry priors and a particle filter to estimate the robot pose relative to the saved map. A lightweight EKF-based odometry correction layer fuses wheel odometry and IMU to produce $\hat{x}_k$ used as motion prior for AMCL. The planner utilizes a time-elastic band (TEB) local planner with velocity smoothing to generate safe velocity commands at $10$ Hz while ensuring that planning latency remains under $15$ ms per cycle in practice.

Equation (2) is the Kalman gain used in our EKF for fusing odometry and IMU-derived angle rates. $P_k^{-}$ denotes the prior covariance, $H$ the observation Jacobian, and $R$ the sensor noise covariance. The proposed module limits correction magnitude to prevent sudden discontinuous jumps in the published /odom topic that could destabilize downstream planners.

We use cross-entropy loss during offline parameter tuning of the visual feature classifier when the RGB-D camera is enabled; Equation (3) summarizes the cross-entropy loss used to tune classifier hyperparameters where $z_i$ and $\hat{z}_i$ are ground-truth and predicted class probabilities respectively. Despite achieving good offline performance, visual features are used only as an augmentation to Lidar in production to limit sensitivity to lighting variations.

content.text: The planner minimizes a quadratic cost as shown in Equation (4), where $Q$ and $R$ are state and input weighting matrices, $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference trajectory, and $u_k$ are control commands. For safety in hospital corridors, we increase $Q$ terms for lateral deviation and set conservative speed bounds. Our method achieves $95.4\%$ map IoU and planning latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$, outperforming the baseline as presented in Table III and Table IV.

content.text: Description of communication approach: Reliable and secure communication was implemented across the hospital LAN. ROS topics are bridged to an MQTT broker for remote monitoring with topic names /robot_status, /map_snapshot, and /telemetry. Time synchronization is enforced via NTP to the hospital time server. We segment robot traffic on a VLAN to separate telemetry from general hospital traffic and configure QoS rules to prioritize /cmd_vel and /emergency_stop topics. The proposed integration supports map upload/download, remote map inspection, and remote emergency stop through a secure web dashboard.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: Overview of experiments conducted: We conducted a comprehensive field evaluation at Wongsonegoro Hospital in Semarang across ten independent mapping runs, multiple localization-only sessions, latency benchmarks, and endurance tests to validate reliability. The experiments evaluate mapping accuracy, localization error, planning latency, and network integration under typical hospital operating conditions.

content.text: Description of test environment, equipment, and conditions: The experimental environment consists of hospital corridors spanning three floors with corridor lengths up to 200 m and multiple T-intersections and patient room entrances. Tests were conducted during daytime and night shifts to capture lighting variability and pedestrian traffic. The robot followed pre-defined routes to create maps and then executed localization-only tests to assess RMSE. We measured latency by instrumenting planner callback times and recording timestamps on the Jetson. All runs were repeated five times per corridor to average out stochastic effects. The hospital provided scheduled windows for mapping to reduce interference with routine operations.

content.text: Main results discussion: We evaluate mapping quality using Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between the produced occupancy grid and a manually curated ground-truth map for each corridor. Localization is evaluated using RMSE in meters between ground-truth pose markers and estimated poses along test trajectories. Planning latency measures the average time to produce velocity commands at 10 Hz. Our method achieves $\mathrm{IoU}=95.4\%$ and localization RMSE $0.12\ \mathrm{m}$. These values are averaged across runs and are reproducible under both day and night conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the Cartographer-based approach with odometry correction provides the best trade-off between accuracy and latency in this hospital environment.

Analysis of results table: As presented in Table III, the proposed system surpasses baselines in both accuracy and latency. The average planning latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ meets the operational requirement of sub-15 ms planning cycles. CPU and GPU utilization figures demonstrate headroom for additional features such as visual augmentation. Map IoU $95.4\%$ indicates high alignment with ground truth maps and supports hospital staff tasks such as route verification and asset tracking.

Despite achieving high accuracy, dynamic obstacles during peak hours introduce transient artifacts that are addressed by our dynamic-object filtering stage in preprocessing.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: Comparison discussion: We compare the proposed method to Method A (GMapping), Method B (AMCL + GMapping tuning), and Method C (ORB-SLAM2 visual). Metrics include accuracy (IoU), latency, and hardware used. The ablation study evaluates contributions from odometry correction, loop-closure frequency, and use of RGB-D augmentation. Results show that odometry correction reduces localization RMSE by 43\% compared to raw odometry, while Cartographer's optimized loop-closure leads to a 6.2\% IoU improvement over GMapping in the hospital corridors.

content.text: Long-running test results and analysis: We executed endurance tests consisting of continuous mapping and patrol cycles for 24 hours with scheduled recharging events and map snapshot uploads to hospital servers. The system sustained average battery endurance of 4.2 hours per run and performed scheduled map saves at 30-minute intervals. Stress testing with high pedestrian traffic resulted in only transient localization degradations that recovered after loop-closure events. We observed no critical software crashes during the 24-hour continuous operation, and average CPU usage remained below 75\%. The hospital IT team reported no adverse interference with hospital network performance when the robot was isolated on its VLAN.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We present ROS-SLAM-Hospital, a ROS-integrated SLAM mapping and deployment for a public service robot operating at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. The proposed approach integrates Cartographer mapping, AMCL localization, and an EKF-based odometry correction layer on a Jetson + STM32 hardware platform. Extensive experiments across ten mapping runs and a 24-hour endurance test show that our method achieves map IoU $95.4\%$, localization RMSE $0.12\ \mathrm{m}$, and average planning latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$, outperforming baseline methods including GMapping and ORB-SLAM2 in the hospital corridors.

Despite achieving high performance, limitations remain. Visual augmentation is constrained by lighting and camera occlusions; some narrow-room configurations may require manual map editing. Network integration depends on hospital IT coordination for VLANs and firewall rules, which may limit out-of-the-box deployment in other institutions. Future work will focus on adaptive dynamic-object rejection to further reduce transient mapping artifacts, federated multi-robot map merging for collaborative logistics, and formal validation of cybersecurity controls in hospital networks. Specific future plans include: 1) integrating lightweight semantic mapping to tag critical hospital areas (pharmacies, isolation wards); 2) extending multi-floor mapping with elevator localization support; and 3) developing a validated operator training package for hospital staff to perform routine map maintenance and safety checks.
